newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada tries to restore pride in its armed forces.
newsitem.headline: Canada tries to restore pride in its armed forces.

text.p: Defence Minister Doug Young unveiled a package of reforms on Tuesday designed to "restore the pride" to a Canadian military battered by scandals from Somalia to Bosnia to its bases at home.

"I deeply regret that the actions of a few have tarnished the public's perception of the magnificent contribution made by our servicemen and women on so many difficult and hazardous missions," Young told a news conference. "Today we begin the process of restoring the pride and a sense of purpose to a vital national institution."

Among 100 proposals he made to Prime Minister Jean Chretien were more independence for military police to investigate and bring charges even at top levels of the military. He also advocated tighter restrictions on alcohol use with abstinence during "periods of concentrated operations" and better training before deployment.
The Canadian military, which had over the past four decades developed a reputation for its peacekeeping abilities, has reeled in the last few years from one embarrassing incident to another.
The scandals embroiled former Chief of Defence Staff Lt. Gen. Jean Boyle and former Defence Minister David Collenette, both of whom resigned last year while protesting their innocence.

Most prominent has been what has become known as the Somali Affair, referring to Canadian peacekeepers' torturing and killing of Somalis in 1993 and the alleged coverup afterwards. Witnesses and lawyers charged during a two-year public inquiry that military police were called in late to investigate the events and were less vigorous in investigating top-ranking officers.

Former Chief Justice Brian Dickson, who headed a panel that drafted a report for Young on the military justice system, said one of the recommendations was to eliminate any difference in the investigation of difference ranks.
"We heard it time and again ... that those of the lower ranks were very closely investigated and those of the higher ranks were not," said Dickson, himself a former artilleryman.

Some allegations, later denied, said beer was involved in the Somali incidents and a military report issued in January said alcohol clearly was involved in sexual and other abuses in 1994 at the Bakovici mental hospital in Bosnia.

Numerous hazing incidents -- initiation rituals -- also tarnished the Canadian Forces' reputation. Videotapes of one ritual showed the elite Canadian Airborne Regiment urinating and defecating on each other. Such revelations, along with the regiment's behaviour in Somalia, forced its disbanding in 1995.

Asked if similar hazings as well as the abuses in Somalia could be prevented by his reforms, Young said he hoped that better training and education would help prevent such incidents. But he said he was more sure that at least justice would be served more quickly and efficiently if they did occur.
The opposition Reform Party's defence spokesman, Bob Mills, dismised Young's package as "fluff" that would do little to get at the top brass.
